column2: It is not fitting to pursue a warrior who has fled from battle — thinking thus, the Nityas then withdrew from the fight.
Their bodies drenched with blood streaming from wounds made by Daitya weapons, the Nityas, exultant with victory, bowed down to the Goddess Shri Lalita.
Thus a great and terrible battle took place there by night; she looked upon the many forms of the Nityas wounded by weapons.
Hearing the news, the great Queen glanced at them with compassion; by that glance alone their wounds were healed.
And Lalita was pleased with the valour of the Nityas.
Makhashatru, Makhaskandi, Simhaghosha, Shiralaka, Laduna, Pattasena, Purajit, Purvamaraka,
Svargashatru, Svargabala, the one called Durga, Svargakantaka, Atimaya, Brihanmaya and the mighty Upamaya —
these were the arrogant, evil-minded sons of the Daitya Bhanda, equal to their father in the might of their arms and like him in form.
They came and worshipped Bhanda's feet with devotion. Looking at them with pleased eyes, the Danava, destroyer of his own race, spoke these words with pride:

O my sons, who on earth is equal to you? By your prowess I conquered the universe long ago.
brahmandpuran:138:53	In battle you angrily dragged by the hair Shakra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti and the noose-bearing Varuna.
brahmandpuran:138:54	You know all missiles and weapons. Yet while you are wide awake, this ruin of our race has come.
brahmandpuran:138:55	Some wily, wicked woman, arrogant in battle, together with many women like herself, is destroying us.
brahmandpuran:138:56	So in battle you must bring her under your control; she must be captured alive by you with your blazing weapons.
brahmandpuran:138:57	To send you, blinded by immeasurable fury, against a single woman is unfitting; yet such is the course of fate.
brahmandpuran:138:58	Bear this one reversal of heroic fame. Having said this, Bhanda, lord of the Daityas, sent them to battle, and sent two hundred akshauhinis to assist them.
The army of two hundred akshauhinis, adorning its chief like a forehead mark, with knitted brows and weapons in hand, marched out from their homes.
At the departure of Bhanda's sons the earth trembled; portents of many kinds appeared and the world was terrified.
The elderly women of the city showered parched grain on those mighty princes as they moved through the streets in their vehicles.
Bards and minstrels sang the praises of the princes, and the women of the city waved auspicious lights at every door.
As they set out it was as if the earth were being split and the sky dragged along, and the ocean seemed to churn.
Taking the army of two hundred akshauhinis, Bhanda's sons, their faces cruel with brows raised in anger, went out from the city.

We shall devour all the Shakti armies in a moment in battle and grind their circles of weapons with sharp arrows.
brahmandpuran:138:66	We shall swiftly quench the ring of the fire-rampart, and quickly take that ill-bred Lalita captive.
Boasting thus to one another with loud heroic speeches, Bhanda's sons reached the vicinity of the fire-rampart.
Blinded by youth and pride, their sight much obstructed, their brows knitted, they raised a mighty lion-roar.
The cosmic egg seemed to split with it, touching the heights, with the force of a terrible thunderclap released by portentous clouds.
The din of that unprecedented great sound shook the ears and minds of the Shaktis.
Arriving, they raised a clamour with their soldiers, and the ranks of celestial cars swooned at the clash of various weapons.
Seeing the young sons of the Daitya Bhanda, like four-armed warriors, come to fight, Bala became curious.
The maiden daughter of Goddess Lalita, who dwelt near her, worthy of worship by all the circles of Shaktis and endowed with valour,
resembling Lalita in form, became angry — she who is always nine years old, the great mine of all knowledge,
her body like the morning sun, her creeper-like form red as red silk, ever present at the footstool of the great Queen,
her life-breath outside herself, her fourth eye. "I shall swiftly destroy those sons of Bhanda who have come."
Having resolved thus, Mother Bala told the great Queen: "Mother, the sons of the great Daitya Bhanda have come to fight.
Being a maiden, I am eager and wish to fight with them; my arms seem to throb with this itch for battle.
This is my play; do not stop it with your objections. I am a child, always fond of games.
For a moment I will delight my heart with the game of battle." Thus requested, the Goddess replied to the maiden:

Dear child, your limbs are very tender; you are nine years old, of new steps and new training in war; you are my only daughter.
brahmandpuran:138:82	Without you I cannot breathe for even a moment; you are my very breath. Do not go into the great battle.
brahmandpuran:138:83	Dandini, Mantrini and crores of other Shaktis are there to fight the battle. Why are you so heedless, child?
Though restrained thus by Goddess Lalita, the maiden, filled with youthful eagerness, again begged to fight.
Seeing her very firm resolve, Shri Lalitambika embraced her tightly in her arms and gave her permission.
Taking one armour from her own armour, she gave it to her, and bestowing weapons from her own weapons, she sent her forth.
The maiden mounted the eared chariot drawn from the great Queen's bow-staff, yoked with hundreds of pairs of swans.
When she set out for battle, all the deities stationed in the tiers bowed with joined palms, holding up rows of swords.
Saluted by them, she descended from the Chakraraja, finest of chariots, to the ground and plunged into the army that was there.
Seeing the maiden coming, flushed with anger, the Mantrini and the Dandanatha spoke to her in alarm:

O daughter of our lord, why have you resolved to fight? Why has the great Queen sent you to battle so untimely?
brahmandpuran:138:92	This is not fitting while the soldiers are present, for you, child, are the embodied life of the Goddess.
brahmandpuran:138:93	Turn back from your zeal for battle; we bow to you. Though they entreated her thus, she went on with firm resolve.
Exceedingly astonished, the Mantrini and the Dandanayika went along with her on either side to protect her.
Then, followed by those two with their great armies, the maiden went out through the gate of the fire-enclosure.
Seated on the eared chariot, accepting the folded palms of salutation of all the Shakti armies with their leaders,
the subduer of foes rushed at the wicked sons of Bhanda. The maiden had no army of her own;
the whole army of Lalita became her army. Then a battle of exceedingly fierce valour began.
The maiden rained nets of arrows on the Daitya lords. The battle that the great Queen's daughter waged with the sons of Bhandasura was envied by gods and Asuras.
The Daitya princes were utterly astonished to see the nine-year-old standing on the eared chariot, scattering circles of arrows.
The attendants, moving about, reported to the great Queen moment by moment the great battle being fought by the child.
The Mantrini and the Dandanatha did not leave her in the battle; becoming spectators, they remained silent.
The maiden, though one in form, appeared separately to each of the Daitya sons, like a series of reflections of the sun.
Piercing their vital points with arrows crested with fire, her face flushed with anger like a red lotus,
while the dwellers of heaven, watching from the sky, exclaimed at the wonder, honoured with many cries of praise by the Mantrini and Dandanatha,
the swift-handed maiden fought. Throughout the whole second day of battle
Lalita's daughter displayed her own strength, piercing all of them by releasing missiles and counter-missiles.
By releasing the Narayana missile, the great Queen's daughter reduced the army of two hundred akshauhinis to ashes in a moment.
Enraged at the destruction of their akshauhinis in a moment, they drew their heavy bows and fell upon her all together.
Then, amid the clamour of the Shaktis and the gods, the maiden released thirty arrows at once.
With swiftness of hand, with thirty crescent-headed arrows, she struck off the heads of Bhanda's thirty sons.
When Bhanda's sons had thus gone to Yama's abode, the sky-dwellers, exceedingly astonished, rained flowers.
And the great Queen's daughter, destroyer of the Asura army, was embraced joyfully and tightly by the Mantrini and the Dandanatha.
At the displays of her valour, which brought victory, the Shaktis danced and filled the three worlds with a tumult of praise.
All the Shakti commanders, led by the Dandanatha, went to report that wonder to the great Queen.
Hearing from them of her daughter's heroic deeds of arms, Goddess Lalitambika was delighted.
The entire circle of Shaktis, and the gods too, were overcome with wonder at her deeds, never seen before.

Who is our mistress, the great Queen? Who is that Dandanayika? Who is that dark Mantrini? And what kind of servitude is ours?
brahmandpuran:139:46	Here, with all of us serving her, what supreme fruit will one woman enjoy in the role of mistress?
brahmandpuran:139:47	We have no need of weapons that pierce the vital points of others; let our fighting, which wounds our bodies with weapons, cease.
brahmandpuran:139:48	In battle death is certain and our lives would be wasted; death will surely come in battle — what proof is needed?
brahmandpuran:139:49	There is no reward for zeal; sleep alone brings happiness; nothing is like idleness in giving rest to the mind.
brahmandpuran:139:50	Knowing us to be such, what will the Queen do? Even her queenship was created by us together.
brahmandpuran:139:51	If we neglect her thus, she will lose her strength; and when her power is gone, what punishment can that Queen give us?
Thus, giving up the battle and throwing down their weapons, the Shaktis at the gate became drowsy, as if reeling with sleep.
Everywhere sluggishness in their duties and great idleness set in, and the whole great camp of the Shaktis grew slack.
The Danava, having made a great device called Jayavighna, obstacle to victory,
and having made the camp dispirited by its power, wished to crush it. When half the night of the second day of battle had passed,
the Daitya Vishukra went out again from the city, surrounded by thirty akshauhinis, and came to the enemy camp.
The sounds of his battle-drums were then heard; yet the Shaktis in the camp remained inactive.
Then the Mantrini and Dandanatha, untouched by the effects of the obstacle-device because of their greatness, became anxious.

Alas, a great calamity and danger has befallen us. By whose influence have the soldiers lost their zeal?
brahmandpuran:139:60	They have thrown aside their weapons and their eagerness, reeling with sleep and drowsiness; they do not heed commands or worship the great Goddess. These Shaktis, without desire, show indifference.
Thus anxious, the Mantrini and Dandanatha mounted the wheel-chariot and spoke to the great Queen.
The Mantrini said: "O Goddess, this is someone's spell; the Shaktis have lost their zeal and do not listen, great Queen, to your command, which sustains the universe.
They are estranged from one another and averse to all their tasks; closed up with sleep and drowsiness, they speak ill words:
'Who is Dandini? Who is Mantrini? Who again is the great Queen? And what is battle?' — so they scoff greatly.
Just at this moment a very mighty enemy is coming, as if splitting heaven and earth with the sound of loud kettledrums.
Great Queen, please do what is fitting here." Having said this, the Mantrini with Dandini bowed down.
Then Goddess Lalita, casting her glance toward the face of Kameshvara, laughed, showing her rows of deep-red teeth.
In the mass of radiance of her smile, someone with the face of an elephant, ichor flowing from his temples, came forth.
Red as a mass of hibiscus flowers, bearing the crescent moon, holding in his ten hands citron, mace, sugarcane bow, trident, Sudarshana discus,
lotus, noose, blue lotus, a sheaf of paddy, the boon-giving gesture, kusha grass and a jewelled pot,
pot-bellied, crested with the moon, trumpeting deeply, embraced by Siddhilakshmi, he bowed to the great Goddess.
Blessed by her, that great Ganapati, the elephant-faced one, rushed out swiftly to break the great Jayavighna device.
Moving about within the enclosure, the elephant-faced one saw the Jayavighna hidden somewhere in secret.
With terrible, unbearable, thunderous strokes of his tusks, the god crushed the great stone of Jayavighna to powder in a moment.
Reducing that device to dust along with the evil deities stationed in it, he hurled it into the sky.
Then, raising a cry of "kilikila," freed from idleness, the Shaktis stood ready to fight with weapons in hand.
That tusk-faced one, with an unchecked roar from his throat, thus destroyed in the night the victory-device the enemy had created.
Hearing this news, Bhanda was agitated and created many elephant-faced beings resembling himself.
Their greatness was sung ahead of them by swarms of bees stirred by the fragrance of the ichor flowing from their temples;
their hands shone as if scattering the filaments of gleaming pomegranate flowers; they were ever ready to drink up the oceans in play.
Amoda and others, attended by Shaktis led by Riddhi — Amoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, Durmukha,
Arighna and Vighnakartri — these six are the leaders of obstacles, lords of seven crores of Herambas.
They marched in front of that great Ganapati into battle; the elephant-faced ones came out from the ring of the fire-rampart
and, with a tumult of angry "hum" sounds, attacked the Danavas, deafening the worlds again with fierce snorts.
The host of the Gana army fell upon the Daitya forces; Gananatha cut down the Danavas with sharp arrows.
There was a battle between Gananatha and the mighty Vishukra, resounding with fierce roars and the twanging of bows.
Knitting his brows and biting his very red lip, Vishukra, bearing his weapons, fought with him in the battle.
With the clash of weapons, the roars of the gods' enemies, the pounding of the hooves of the Daitya horses like pickaxes,
the trumpeting of great elephants, cries of fear, the neighing of the lines of horses, the rumble of chariot wheels,
the twang of bowstrings and the screech of wheels,
the whizz of arrows, the heroic boasts, the loud laughter of the great lords and many lion-roars,
that fierce battle grew, shaking the directions. The army of thirty akshauhinis of the wicked Vishukra
was fought by each of the Gana lords, great chariot-warriors, piercing vital points with their tusks and holding them fast with their trunks,
enraging them with the flapping of their ears like the Pushkalavarta clouds, scattering the army with harsh blasts from their nostrils,
crushing them with chests like mountain ramparts, grinding them with stamping feet and striking them with their stout bellies,
piercing with tridents, cutting with the fall of discuses, terrifying the army with the great blast of the conch —
thousands of elephant-faced ones born from Gananatha's mouth, with great effort, reduced that entire army to dust.
Then, filled with anger, the leader of his army sent the Asura Gaja against the god.
That lord of the Ganas fought the evil-minded Gaja Daitya, who roared a fierce lion-roar and was accompanied by seven akshauhinis.
Seeing the strength of Gajasura's arms decline and the god's might increase, Vishukra fled.
That lord of heroes, alone, moving on his mouse mount, crushed Gajasura along with his seven akshauhinis.
When Gajasura was slain and Vishukra had fled, the great Ganapati came from the battle to Lalita's side.
That night, which had been the night of doom for the Daityas, came to an end, and Lalita was greatly delighted with his valour.
The great Queen, well pleased, granted the lord of the Ganas the supreme privilege of being worshipped first in the worship of all the gods.

Our army is being weakened — alas, the course of fate! Their palates dried, the lustre of their weapons fallen, the circle of Shaktis has become neglectful in this battle.
brahmandpuran:140:51	None of them fights or holds a weapon; with their palates dry, my friend, they are not even able to speak.
brahmandpuran:140:52	Hearing of our plight, what will the great Goddess say? The Daityas have done us harm; let a remedy be thought out.
brahmandpuran:140:53	Everywhere here, O Potrini, in the sixteen thousand akshauhinis there is not a single Shakti who is not tormented by thirst.
brahmandpuran:140:54	At this very moment, seeing the army with weapons laid down, the Danavas, striking at the weak point, are killing them with arrows.
brahmandpuran:140:55	A remedy must be found by you, and by me in the effort of battle. The great cool ocean that is in a tier of your chariot —
brahmandpuran:140:56	command it to quench the thirst of all the Shaktis. Their thirst will not be relieved by small drinks of water and the like.
brahmandpuran:140:57	That ocean of wine alone will satisfy the host of Shaktis. Command that great one who rouses zeal for battle, who quenches all thirst and greatly increases strength.
When this was said, the Dandanatha, delighted with the good remedy, summoned the ocean of nectar and gave the command in battle as Chakreshvari.
He, his eyes red and languid with intoxication, golden in hue and adorned with garlands,
bowing to the Dandanatha and obeying her command,
making himself manifold — in places red as the young sun, in places dark as the tapichchha tree, in places of white lustre —
this king of oceans, multiplied by the wind, rained crores of sweet streams shaped like elephants' trunks.
Sprinkled by the Pushkalavarta and other clouds of the end of the kalpa, the ocean fell into the middle of the Shakti army.
The ocean of wine rained that by whose mere fragrance the dead would surely rise and the weak become strong.
Those streams of wine, beyond counting even by parardhas, the Shaktis arose and drank with mouths parched by thirst.
So that the shower from the ocean of wine would not fall on the Daityas, the dweller in the kadamba forest,
causing wonder, made a great ring of ramparts around the army with thousands of arrows released with swift hands.
By that deed all the gods were amazed. Then those Shaktis drank abundantly in the midst of battle
various streams of wine that increased strength and zeal, each according to her own liking, taste and relish.
On the third day of battle, for two watches, the ocean of wine rained unceasingly in streams of liquor.
Gaudi, Paishti, Madhvi, the excellent Kadambari, Haitali, Langaleya, and wines made from palm,
divine wines born of the wish-granting tree and from various lands, very tasty and fragrant, giving pleasant scents and joy,
fragrant like bakula blossoms, fizzing and bright with bubbles, pungent, astringent, sweet and touched with bitterness,
of many colours, cleansing and slimy, slightly sour, pungent-sour and sweet-sour,
one that heals the pain of weapon-wounds and one that joins broken bones, cool ones that remove battle fatigue, light ones and warm ones,
and Varunis that remove fever and grant victory — such various streams of wine the ocean of wine rained down.
For a full watch without break, each Yogini there joyfully drank a stream of wine like the trunk of Airavata.
Turning their faces upward, their tongues darting, the Shaktis drank the wine joyfully with half-closed eyes.
Having thus satisfied them with many kinds of streams of wine, the ocean of nectar took on a divine form.
The ocean of wine went again to the Dandanatha, bowed, and said this to her in a smooth, deep voice:
Seeing the Shaktis thus pointed out by the ocean of wine, Dandini was greatly pleased and said to him:

I am well pleased, O ocean of wine; you have given help. Moreover, this work of the gods has been freed from obstacles by you.
brahmandpuran:140:87	Henceforth, by my grace, in the Dvapara age you will be used by sacrificers in their rites exceedingly, like the drinking of Soma.
brahmandpuran:140:88	All the deities will drink you purified by mantra in sacrifice; and people, drinking you purified by mantra in sacrifices,
brahmandpuran:140:89	will attain success, prosperity, strength, heaven and liberation. The great Goddess, Mahadeva, Baladeva, the Bhargava, Dattatreya, Brahma and Vishnu — these great ones will drink you.
brahmandpuran:140:90	Worshipped in sacrifice, you will grant every success.
Having pleased the ocean of wine by granting him this boon,
Dandini urged the Mantrini on to battle again. Once more battle began between the Shaktis and the Danavas.
Splitting the mountains of the eight directions with joyful loud laughter, intoxicated with fresh wine, their eyes reddened, the Shaktis fell upon the circles of Daityas all at once.
In two ways the Shaktis, glorious in their intoxication, shone red: their eyes with the flush of wine, and their swords with the blood of the Daityas.
The battle between the Shaktis and the gods' enemies became so tumultuous that it was as if Death, unafraid, were himself destroying creatures.
Their steps faltering, their eyes red with intoxication, their heroic words slurred, arrogant in battle,
shaped like kadamba balls, eyes gleaming on every limb, the Shaktis destroyed the armies of the crown prince.
There Dandini tore apart a hundred akshauhinis; the Mantrini destroyed a hundred and fifty akshauhinis.
Ashvarudha and the others, their eyes red with intoxication, led a hundred and fifty akshauhinis to the house of Death.
With her very sharp goad, the horse-riding Rohini crushed Ulukajit in battle and made him a guest of the other world.
The Shakti commanders of the staff, led by Sampatkari, blocked others with harsh force and tore them apart.
When the sun had set, Shyamala, full of anger, fought Vishukra, whose entire army had been destroyed.
With the release of missiles and counter-missiles, terrifying to the gods, the Mantrini fought him in a great display of warfare.
Cutting in turn the very sharp weapons of the mighty Vishukra, his banner and his charioteer,
cutting with arrows his bowstring and bow-staff, with the Brahmashiras missile blazing like fire
she crushed Vishukra, and he fell with his body shattered. And the Dandanatha, exultant, fought the great Daitya Vishanga,
striking him fiercely with her pestle. That wicked Danava too raised in his arm a mace like the staff of death and fought a battle terrifying to all.
Crushing each other's limbs, engaged in mace combat, loud with fierce laughter, circling about,
making various movements, whirling and weaving swiftly, stunning each other again and again with blows of their staffs,

striking each other and watching for an opening, exceedingly fierce, shaking the sky with the clash of the tips of their great pestle and mace, the unassailable Dandini and the chief of the Daityas fought.
Then, having fought until midnight, the Dandanayika, enraged, began to kill Vishanga.
Dragging the enemy with her plough sunk into his head, Potrini then struck him a hard blow with her pestle.
Then, his life gone from the blow of the pestle, the great Asura fell to the ground together with his shattered chariot.
Having done this great deed, the Mantrini and the Dandanayika spent the rest of that night there and returned to the camp.
Bowing to that great Queen, and appointed to destroy the diseases of her devotees in the three worlds, they went to their own stations.
The Danava Bhanda released the life-destroying missile; the Queen released the missile in the form of Kalasankarshani.
The Danava Bhanda released the fearsome Mahasura missile; from it arose thousands of huge-bodied, mighty ones:
Madhu and Kaitabha, Mahishasura, the Daitya Dhumralochana, the Asuras Chanda, Munda and others,
Chikshura, Chamara, the Asura Raktabija, Shumbha and Nishumbha, and the mighty Kalakeyas,
and others called the Dhumras arose from that missile. All those foremost Danavas, with harsh circles of weapons,
crushing the Shakti army and roaring terribly — the Shaktis, crushed by the Daityas, crying "Alas!"
quickly took refuge in Lalita, crying "Save us, save us!" Then the Goddess, greatly enraged, let out a loud laugh of fury.
From it arose a glorious one named Durga, fashioned from the splendour of all the gods, of universal form.
She bore the trident given by the trident-bearer, the discus offered by the discus-bearer, the conch given by Varuna, the spear given by Agni,
the bow and inexhaustible quivers given by the Wind in the great battle, the thunderbolt given by the wielder of the thunderbolt, the cup offered by the lord of wealth,
the great staff of death, the noose given by the noose-bearer, the water-pot given by Brahma, the bell offered by Airavata,
the sword and shield given by Death, the necklace offered by the ocean, and ornaments given by Vishvakarman.
With limbs shining with rays like rows of thousand-rayed suns, lighting up all the weapons with great radiance,
beautiful with other accoutrements given by others, mounting the lion, Narayani gave battle.
Thus those Danavas like Mahisha were struck down, just as she had done long ago in the Chandika Saptashati.
In the same way she fought the battle that crushed the pride of Mahisha and the rest. Having done that difficult deed, she bowed to Lalita.
The wicked Danava released the Muka (dumbness) missile against the Shakti army; the Mother of the world released the missile named Mahavagvadini.
The arrogant Danava Bhanda released in that battle the base Asuras who steal the Veda, whose form is knowledge.
They were countered by the great Queen from the thumbnail of her right hand. The great hero Bhanda then released the Ocean missile in battle.
The Shakti army sank in its overflowing flood. Then from the nail of the forefinger of Shri Lalita's right hand arose the primal Tortoise, a yojana in extent.
Held up by his vast shell, the Shaktis rejoiced and lost their fear of the Ocean missile.
And the Lord drank up all that ocean water. The wicked Danava then released the great Hiranyaksha missile.
From it were born thousands of Hiranyakshas bearing maces. As the Shakti army, being struck by them, grew terrified and distressed, scattered here and there, and slackened in battle,
then from the nail of the middle finger of Shri Lalita's right hand arose the Great Boar, white like Kailasa.
Torn apart by that boar with its tusk like a thunderbolt, those crores of Hiranyakshas were crushed and destroyed.
Then Bhanda in great anger knitted his brows; from his frown were born crores of Hiranyas,
blazing like the burning sun and bearing flaming weapons; they crushed the Shakti army and crushed Prahlada as well.
The Prahlada that belongs to the Shaktis, marked by supreme bliss, became a child, tormented by Hiranya,
and took refuge in Lalita; so the Queen felt compassion. Then, to protect Prahlada, whose form is the bliss of Shakti,
the great Goddess shook the tip of the ring finger of her right hand. From it arose, with shaking mane and three blazing eyes,
lion-faced and man-shaped below the neck, Janardana, armed with claws, in the form of Kalarudra, with terrible loud laughter,
with a thousand mighty arms, obeying Lalita's command; all the Hiranyakashipus born from Bhanda's frown
he tore apart in a moment with claws harsh as the thunderbolt. Goddess Lalita released against the great Asura Bhanda the very terrible Balindra missile, which destroys all the gods.
To destroy the pride of that missile, hundreds of Vamanas arose from the tip of the little finger of the great Queen's right hand, of great might,
growing moment by moment, mighty, noose in hand, binding with nooses the Balindras born of the missile.
Born from the tip of the little finger of the right hand, the consorts of Kamesha, huge-bodied and very zealous, destroyed that missile.
The Daitya Bhanda released the Haihaya missile on the battlefield; from it were born thousands and crores of Sahasrarjunas.
Then from the thumbnail of Shri Lalita's left hand arose Rama the Bhargava, blazing, wrathful, roaring like a lion,
and cleaving them with the hard edge of his axe, he destroyed those countless Sahasrarjunas in a moment.
Then the Daitya Bhanda in anger let out a "hum"; from that "hum" was born one bearing the Chandrahasa sword,
surrounded by a Rakshasa army of a thousand akshauhinis; taking his younger brother Kumbhakarna and his son Meghanada, he crushed the Shakti army far and wide.
Then from the nail of the forefinger of Shri Lalita's left hand arose Rama of the bow, accompanied by Lakshmana,
wearing a crown of matted hair, a quiver tied with creepers on his back, dark as a blue lotus petal, twanging his bow again and again.
With divine missiles he destroyed the Rakshasa army in a moment; he crushed the son of Pulastya and his brother Kumbhakarna, and Lakshmana destroyed the great hero Meghanada.
The Danava Bhanda released the very terrible Dvivida missile; from it were born countless monkeys with tawny eyes,
their faces deep red with anger, each equal to Hanuman; with cruel shrieks they destroyed the Shakti army.
Then from the nail of the middle finger of Shri Lalita's left hand appeared the one whose emblem is the palm tree, his eyes red with anger,
his body clothed in blue garments, pure as Mount Kailasa; he destroyed all the monkeys born of the Dvivida missile.
The mighty one released the great missile named Rajasura; from that missile arose many Danava kings:
Shishupala, Dantavaktra, Shalva, the king of Kashi, Paundraka Vasudeva, Rukmi, Dimbhaka and Hamsaka,
Shambara, Pralamba, the Asura Bana, Kamsa, the wrestler Chanura, Mushtika and Utpalashekhara,
Arishta, Dhenuka, Keshin, Kaliya, the twin Arjuna trees, Putana, Shakata, Trinavarta and other Asuras,
the great hero called Naraka and the Asura Mura in Vishnu's form — many arose with their armies, weapons in hand.
To destroy them all, the eternal Vasudeva, born from the nail of the ring finger of the Goddess's left lotus hand,
formed the fourfold manifestation, and they became four: Vasudeva, the second remembered as Sankarshana,
Pradyumna and Aniruddha, all with weapons raised; those evil ones, causes of the earth's burden,
great Asuras disguised as kings, they destroyed completely.
When they had perished, the Danava Bhanda, enraged, released the terrible Kali missile, destroyer of dharma.
From the Kali missile were born Andhra and Pundra kings, Kiratas, Shabaras, Hunas and Yavanas of sinful conduct,
destroyers of the Veda, enemies of dharma, killers of living beings, causing confusion among the classes and stages of life, foul in body; again and again they crushed the armies of Lalita's Shaktis.
Then from the nail of the little finger of Shri Lalita's radiant left lotus hand arose Janardana named Kalki,
mounted on a horse, blazing with glory, and he laughed aloud. By that very sound, like the crash of a thunderbolt,
the Kiratas swooned and perished, and the Shaktis rejoiced. Those lords of the ten incarnations, having done this difficult deed,
bowed to Lalita and stood with joined palms. Appointed by Mother Lalita to protect dharma in every kalpa through births as the Fish and the others, they departed for Vaikuntha.
When all his missiles had thus been destroyed, the evil one released the Mahamoha missile, and by it the Shaktis swooned.

The Mother, releasing the Shambhava missile, destroyed the Mahamoha missile. As the great battle went on thus with streams of missiles and counter-missiles, the ruddy lord of rays began to go to the setting mountain.
Then with the Narayana missile Goddess Lalitambika reduced all his akshauhinis to ashes in the battle.
Then with the Pashupata missile, radiant like the blazing fire of doom, the great Queen crushed his forty army commanders.
Then he alone remained, the wicked one whose kinsmen had all been slain, blazing with anger, destroyer of the world —
the great Asura of great strength, Bhanda of fierce valour — the Mother, Lalita the supreme Queen, deprived him of life with the great Kameshvara missile, radiant as a thousand suns.
Overwhelmed by the flames of that missile, his city Shunyaka, with its women and children, its cattle, wealth and grain,
was burned down at once, and only the bare ground remained. At the destruction of Bhanda the three worlds danced with joy.

Having thus accomplished the work of the gods, she of blameless conduct, the glory adorning the circle of the Shrichakra chariot, Kameshvari, Mother of the three worlds, shone, radiant in her greatness and rich in the glory of victory.
When the sun had set, the Goddess of renowned power brought back to her camp the whole army, wearied by the labour of battle and scorched by the fire of Bhandasura's mighty arrows.

O lord of ascetics, whoever reads even once this slaying of the Danava Bhanda accomplished by Lalitamba — his troubles perish, the eight perfections are his, and both enjoyment and liberation lie in his hand.
Those men who read on holy days this purifying account of Lalita's valour, which destroys all sins and grants every perfection, attain supreme good fortune and prosperity.
For those whose minds are devoted to my worship and to my devotees, bring about all the pleasures of love they desire.
Receiving this command of Goddess Lalita, Smara said "So be it," bearing it on his head, and went forth with joined palms.
From all the pores of that bodiless one arose many beautiful Madanas who bewitch the universe.
Having bewitched the whole circle of the world with them, the mind-born one went again to the hermitage of Sthanu, desiring to conquer the moon-crested god,
with his friend Spring, with the cool-rayed moon as his general, with Passion as his companion and the swift gentle breeze,
accompanied by trumpets in the form of the calls of male cuckoos, rich in the sentiments of love and heroism, his body embraced by Rati,
brandishing his victorious bow, foremost among heroes, he reached the presence of the enemy of Love and stood fearless.
He struck the moon-crested one, absorbed in austerity, with his arrows. Struck by the floods of Kandarpa's arrows, the moon-crested one cast off his dispassion and abandoned his hard austerity.
Giving up all his observances, Shiva was made to lose his composure; meditating on that Parvati alone, again and again, stricken by love,
Sharva sighed, his cheeks turning pale; tearful, separated from his beloved, burning with the loss of his composure, again and again remembering the daughter of the mountain whom he had seen before.
For the trident-bearer, burning with the fire of the bodiless one's arrows, neither the crescent moon nor the Ganga could relieve the heat of his body.
On a bed of flowers brought by the circles of his Ganas led by Nandi, Bhringi and Mahakala, he tossed again and again.
Taking Nandi's hand, from one flower-bed to another, he went and writhed again and again.
Neither by the bed of flowers nor by the nectar flowing from the crescent moon nor by icy waters was the fever of his body relieved.
To quench the great flame in his body, Shiva lay again and again upon slabs of frozen ice-water; again he drew with his nails the form of the mountain's daughter on a painting cloth.
Looking at it only increased his pangs of love. Having drawn her bowed with modesty and looking sidelong,
he pressed that painting to his limbs, which bristled with thrill. With great preoccupation, with great longing for the joy of love, and with the intense heat of love, the odd-eyed god suffered.
Seeing her everywhere, directing his mind to her alone, talking with her as if in a frenzy,
his heart consisting of her alone, his mind on her, wholly devoted to her, passing all his nights and days in the nectar of stories about her,
delighting in describing her character, eager to see her form, weaving garlands of flowers of imagined sweet enjoyment with her — having become absorbed in her, Shiva suffered exceedingly.
The one with matted locks, seeing this incurable sickness of love, became very eager for marriage.
Having thus bewitched that god at Lalita's command, Kandarpa then tormented the mountain's daughter with his arrows.
With hot sighs darkened by the intense flames of separation, her lip-petals dried up and her cheeks grew very pale.
